summary: Specifies the Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior for Differentiated Services, which protects best-effort traffic from lower-effort traffic during congestion. It can also serve as a scavenger service class. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some traffic is less urgent. This marks it so when the network gets crowded, it waits for everything else.

questions: what is the lower effort phb
why not use cs1 for low priority traffic
subtitle: A traffic class for data that should only use the network when nobody else wants it.

tldr.problem: Some traffic, such as backups and software updates, is not urgent, yet it competes with ordinary best-effort traffic when links are busy. The older recommendation to mark it with CS1 could even make it win over best-effort traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The Lower-Effort (LE) Per-Hop Behavior gives packets lower precedence than the default PHB, so they are dropped first in congestion and may be starved. RFC 8622 recommends the new DSCP 000001 for it.
tldr.outcome: Best-effort traffic keeps priority over LE traffic, so LE cannot crowd it out. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3662 and moves RFC 4594 and RFC 8325 from CS1 to the LE codepoint.

today: RFC 8622 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3662 and updates RFC 4594 and RFC 8325 to use the LE codepoint.

sections.title: What the LE PHB Is
sections.content:
RFC 8622 defines the Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior (LE PHB) for Differentiated Services. It is meant for traffic of such low urgency that all other traffic takes precedence over it when using link bandwidth. The RFC compares it to a background priority for processes in an operating system. Low urgency does not mean the traffic is unimportant.

LE packets scavenge resources nobody else is using, which is where the early Internet2 name "scavenger service" came from. Two properties follow: the traffic should use spare capacity, and it must be preemptable by the default PHB or other elevated PHBs. That gives the no harm property: LE traffic has a strictly limited effect on all other traffic.

LE is distinct from Best-Effort (BE). BE gets an implied good-faith commitment of at least some resources, while the network makes no commitment to deliver LE packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a queue where the polite kids let everyone else go first. LE traffic is the polite kid: it only goes when the road is empty.

sections.title: When to Use LE
sections.content:
LE suits traffic that can tolerate strongly varying throughput, including long stretches of very low throughput or complete starvation. Applications should expect LE packets to be badly delayed or dropped whenever other traffic is present. The RFC lists uses such as search engine crawling, software updates, telemetry and error reports, backups and mirroring, cache-to-cache content distribution, prefetching, and multicast from untrusted sources.

LE traffic SHOULD still be congestion controlled, and transports should detect starvation and resume rather than give up, for example with exponential back-off with an upper bound. LE SHOULD NOT be used for a customer's normal Internet traffic, and packets SHOULD NOT be downgraded to LE instead of being dropped, particularly when they are unauthorized.

One operator use is filling capacity normally kept spare. Some providers keep link utilization below 50% so traffic survives rerouting after a link failure. LE traffic can use that capacity and is preempted automatically when all of the link is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: It is good for jobs that can pause, like a big download overnight. It is bad for a video call, which cannot wait.

sections.title: How Routers Treat LE Packets
sections.content:
A packet forwarded with the LE PHB SHOULD have lower precedence than default-PHB packets: in congestion, LE traffic is dropped before any default traffic. Ideally, LE packets are forwarded only when no packet of any other PHB is waiting, so they can be starved completely. A scheduler can reflect the operator's policy about that.

The simplest implementation is a priority scheduler that serves the default queue ahead of an LE queue. A scheduler that gives LE a very small weight is another option, though it can sometimes serve LE better than BE when the BE share is full and the LE share is not. Without a dedicated queue, active queue management in a shared BE/LE queue can drop arriving LE packets once a queue length or sojourn time threshold is exceeded.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) SHOULD be used for LE packets too, including Congestion Experienced marking of ECT-marked packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The router has a fast line and a slow line. The slow line only moves when the fast line is empty.

sections.title: The Recommended Codepoint
sections.content:
The recommended DSCP for LE is 000001 (decimal 1). Earlier specifications such as RFC 4594 recommended Class Selector 1 (CS1). The RFC calls that problematic: in Diffserv domains that treat CS1 as originally proposed in RFC 2474, it causes a priority inversion, forwarding LE packets with higher precedence than BE packets. Existing implementations SHOULD move to the new codepoint when possible.

The value was picked using measurements of DSCP re-marking behavior in the Internet. Some domains set the old IP Precedence bits to zero, so a codepoint from the Standards Action Pool 1 (xxxxx0) might get other standardized DSCPs mapped onto LE. IANA registered LE in Pool 3 (xxxx01, Standards Action) to avoid other flows accidentally becoming LE through partial DSCP bleaching.
sections.plainLanguage: The old label looked a lot like a label for slightly important mail, so it caused mix-ups. The new label is its own thing.

sections.title: Deployment and Re-marking
sections.content:
A DS node needs only a behavior-aggregate classifier that recognizes the LE DSCP, a dedicated LE queue, and a suitable scheduler such as simple priority queueing. LE has no parameters, needs no traffic profiles, and requires no meters, droppers or shapers. Because it cannot harm other traffic, providers can trust LE markings from end systems without policing or re-marking them.

A domain that does not support LE SHOULD NOT drop LE packets. It SHOULD treat them as the default PHB while keeping the LE DSCP, so later domains can still honor it. DSCP bleaching to 000000 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Mapping LE to the default PHB breaks the no-harm property, and policing the LE aggregate MAY be used to limit the effect. Applications that want lower precedence even then should use a lower-than-best-effort transport such as LEDBAT.

A domain still using CS1 for low-priority data SHOULD re-mark it to 000001 at egress to the next domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If a town has no slow line, it should still treat the packet normally but leave the label on, so the next town can still use it.

sections.title: Updates to Other RFCs
sections.content:
Section 10 changes RFC 4594: every occurrence of CS1 for Low-Priority Data is replaced by LE, in its Figure 3, Figure 4, the notes and Section 4.10. It also drops the old advice to re-mark such traffic to 000xx1 in IP Precedence networks, because the LE DSCP makes that unnecessary.

Section 11 changes RFC 8325 so that Low-Priority Data marked LE, or legacy CS1, maps to UP 1 (AC_BK, Background). RFC 3662, which defined Lower Effort as a per-domain behavior, is obsoleted.

Section 9 adds multicast cautions: replication can exhaust internal forwarding resources before a packet reaches a full LE output queue, so conditional replication is suggested, though the RFC says it is probably not widely implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: This document also fixes the label on two older rulebooks so they all agree.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC finds no specific security exposures for the PHB itself. Since LE is a low-priority class, an attacker who can change a packet's DSCP to LE can carry out a downgrade attack that degrades its quality of service.

On privacy, an observer could infer from the DSCP that traffic is low urgency. That may help an observer focus on other traffic, and a user could hide interesting traffic in the LE aggregate. The RFC judges the impact of this disclosure likely negligible in most cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad guy could stick the slow-line label on your packets to make them late. Also, the label tells watchers that your packet is not in a hurry.
